Threat: Credential stuffing / brute force / password spraying
Source Refs: ATT&CK T1110, CWE-307, ASVS 5.0 V6 Authentication
Abuse Case: Attacker replays breached credential lists against login, or sprays one common password across many accounts so no single account trips its own counter; the code resend, the MFA challenge and the invite endpoint are hit the same way and are usually left unthrottled
Required Controls: Rate-limit per account and per source, and separately on the failure rate across accounts so spraying is visible where a per-account counter is not; lockout with jitter; breached-password check; MFA; throttle the one-time-code resend, the MFA challenge and the invite endpoint like the login itself, and never let a resend reset the failure counter; recovery stays reachable while an account is throttled, so throttling is not a denial of service against the owner; admit the verifier's cost for an unknown identity too, so response time does not say which addresses exist
Negative Tests: Test: >N failed logins -> 429/lockout; lockout not bypassable via case-variant email, a Unicode-equivalent address, or a rotated source address; one password tried across many accounts trips the cross-account rate; a code resend does not reset the counter; response time for a known and an unknown identity is not separable. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - nothing here exercises a consumer's login endpoint; the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Abuse Case: Attacker fixes a session id pre-login or reuses one post-logout/password-change
Required Controls: Rotate session id on login + privilege change; invalidate all sessions on password reset
Negative Tests: Test: session id differs pre/post login; old token rejected after reset

Abuse Case: Attacker enumerates/reuses reset tokens or intercepts via referrer leak
Required Controls: Single-use, short-TTL, hashed-at-rest tokens; uniform response on unknown email; no token in URL logs
Negative Tests: Test: token unusable twice; expired token rejected; response identical for known/unknown email

Threat: Account enumeration through an observable difference
Source Refs: CWE-204, CWE-203, CWE-208, ASVS 5.0 V6 Authentication
Abuse Case: The login, reset, sign-up or verification response says whether an email address is already registered: a different message, status code, redirect target or cookie, or an early return before the verifier runs, tells the attacker which account exists
Required Controls: One response shape for known and unknown identities at every identity entry point; the verifier path runs for an unknown identity too; sign-up for an address that already exists returns the same response as a new one and mails the owner a notice instead; a deliberately disclosing flow is a written project decision recorded with the flow, never a default and never a defect when it is written down
Negative Tests: Test: a known and an unknown identity produce the same status, body category, redirect and cookies on login, reset request, sign-up and verification resend; sign-up for a registered address emits a notice to the owner and no distinguishing response. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - nothing here runs a consumer's identity flow; the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite, written as the equivalence case test-case-discovery names

Abuse Case: An address nobody proved they control reaches a privileged state: sign-up grants access before verification, a mail scanner's GET on the verification or magic link consumes it before the person sees it, or two concurrent requests both spend a verification token that was never single-use
Required Controls: No privilege before proven ownership; the link's GET is safe and the state change needs an explicit confirmation a scanner will not perform; the token is single-use, short-lived and consumed atomically under concurrency; a resend invalidates the previous token; changing the address returns the account to the unverified state
Negative Tests: Test: an account whose address is unverified cannot reach the privileged action; a plain GET on the verification link does not consume it; two concurrent consumptions of one token yield exactly one success; a resend makes the previous token unusable. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Threat: Password acceptance weakened by composition and handling rules
Abuse Case: Composition rules, forced periodic rotation, a low maximum length, a blocked paste or a missing breached-and-common screen push people towards predictable passwords the attacker already holds
Required Controls: Accept the length and character range the authority sets, without composition rules and without scheduled rotation; rotate on evidence of compromise only; allow paste and password managers; screen against a breached-and-common list; normalise Unicode before the check; every value defers to ASVS 5.0 V6 Authentication and NIST SP 800-63B, never to this corpus
Negative Tests: Test: a long passphrase and a pasted password are accepted; a password on the breached list is refused with a reason the person can act on; no scheduled expiry forces a change. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite against the authority named in Required Controls

Source Refs: CWE-916, CWE-759, ASVS 5.0 V6 Authentication, ASVS 5.0 V11 Cryptography
Abuse Case: Passwords stored under a general-purpose hash, salted or not, or under a hand-rolled salt scheme, so a stolen table is cracked at speed; or an over-long input is silently truncated at the algorithm's own limit; or the pepper sits in the repository or in the same store as the hash
Required Controls: A password hashing function the authority names, with its parameters taken from the authority and never from this corpus; never a general-purpose hash - MD5, SHA-1 and every SHA-2 included, salted or not - and never an invented salt scheme; the salt is per-password and generated by the library; rehash on a successful login once the parameters have moved; refuse or pre-digest an input past the algorithm's own length limit rather than truncating it; a pepper, where one is used, lives outside the credential store with a rotation plan and is never a literal in the tree - its absence is not a finding
Negative Tests: Test: the stored value is produced by the platform's password hashing API and checked through its verify primitive, never by comparing digests; an input past the algorithm's limit is refused or pre-digested, never silently cut; a login under outdated parameters rewrites the stored value. Decided by: PARTIAL CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - ai-code-blindspots carries a password-scoped fast-hash grep that catches the authoring-time shape; the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite and static analysis

Threat: Unsafe secret comparison and home-made credential primitives
Abuse Case: A token, one-time code, signature or MAC compared with the language's ordinary equality leaks its prefix through timing; or the project mints its own token or one-time code from a non-cryptographic source an attacker can predict from a seed
Required Controls: Compare every secret with the platform's constant-time primitive and respect that primitive's length precondition; draw every token, one-time code and salt from the platform's cryptographically secure random source; never invent a credential primitive where the library ships one
Negative Tests: Test: no equality operator compares a token, one-time code, signature or MAC anywhere on the identity path; codes drawn repeatedly show no sequence reproducible from a seed. Decided by: PARTIAL CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - ai-code-blindspots carries a raw-secret-equality grep that catches the authoring-time shape; the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite and static analysis

Source Refs: CWE-640, CWE-362, ASVS 5.0 V6 Authentication, ASVS 5.0 V7 Session Management
Abuse Case: The reset link is built from an attacker-controlled Host header, or leaks through the Referrer of a third-party asset on the reset page; or the reset signs the person straight in, leaves the other sessions alive, satisfies the second factor, or is spent twice by concurrent requests
Required Controls: Build the link from server configuration, never from a request header; no third-party asset and no secret in the query string on the reset page; the reset ends every other session and the remembered-device state; it does not sign the person in and does not satisfy the second factor; single use enforced atomically under concurrency; the owner is notified on the channel that was already verified
Negative Tests: Test: a forged Host header does not change the link's origin; the reset page loads no third-party asset; after a reset the pre-reset session token is rejected and a second factor is still demanded; two concurrent uses of one token yield exactly one success. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Threat: Identity or credential change without fresh re-authentication or notice
Source Refs: CWE-620, CWE-778, ASVS 5.0 V6 Authentication, ASVS 5.0 V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
Abuse Case: A hijacked session can change the account's email address, phone number, password, MFA factor, passkey, recovery codes or a linked identity without proving the person is still present, and nobody is told: the channel that was already verified gets no notice, and a sign-in from an unrecognised device is silent
Required Controls: Every identity mutation demands fresh re-authentication at the assurance the factor being changed already carries; the previously verified address or number is notified and the change is reversible for a window the project states; a sign-in from an unrecognised device notifies the owner; each event is logged with actor, time and outcome, and never with the secret
Negative Tests: Test: each identity mutation refuses without a fresh re-authentication, and a lower-assurance factor does not satisfy it; the previously verified channel receives the notice; the log line for each event carries no credential substring. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Threat: MFA enforced only in the interface or undercut by its recovery path
Abuse Case: The second factor is a screen the client can skip because the server already issued a full session; or the recovery path is weaker than the factor it replaces; or the TOTP seed sits in the credential store in plaintext and the backup codes are stored unhashed or stay valid after use
Required Controls: The server issues no privileged session until the factor is verified - the challenge is a state the server holds, not a screen the client renders; recovery is at least as strong as the factor it replaces, and is itself throttled and notified; the shared seed is encrypted at rest under a key held outside the credential store; backup codes are hashed like passwords and are single-use; enrolling or removing a factor is an identity mutation under its own row
Negative Tests: Test: a request that skips the challenge step reaches no privileged action; a backup code fails on its second use; the stored seed is not readable from the credential store alone. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Source Refs: CWE-613, CWE-539, ASVS 5.0 V7 Session Management
Abuse Case: A remember-me token lifted from a device reaches a sensitive action without a fresh login; or logout clears the client and leaves the server session, the remembered-device record and the federated session alive
Required Controls: A remembered session carries a lower assurance and never satisfies a sensitive action on its own; the remember-me token is per-device, rotated on use, and revocable from a session list the owner can see; logout invalidates the server-side state, the remember-me record and the cookie, and offers to end the federated session too; every session ends on a credential change
Negative Tests: Test: a remembered session is re-challenged at a sensitive action; after logout the previous token is rejected server-side, not merely absent from the client; revoking a device from the session list rejects that device's token. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Threat: Authentication token in script-readable browser storage
Abuse Case: A session, access or refresh token is written to localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB or another store page script can read, so any injected script reads it and replays it from the attacker's own device for as long as the token lives
Required Controls: Carry the session in a cookie marked HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite, which page script cannot read; never persist a session, access or refresh token in Web Storage or IndexedDB; where an architecture requires a script-held bearer token, keep it in memory only, short-lived and narrowly scoped, and treat that as shortening the exposure rather than preventing theft during a script compromise; a cookie-borne session still needs the login and state-changing CSRF controls of its own rows
Negative Tests: Test: after sign-in and after the federated callback, no session, access or refresh token value is present in localStorage, sessionStorage or IndexedDB, whether written with setItem or by property assignment; the session cookie carries HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite. Decided by: check_account_surface reports the setItem and property-assignment writes lexically; the deciding check is the consumer's own browser test suite

Source Refs: CWE-287, CWE-352, ASVS 5.0 V10 OAuth and OIDC
Abuse Case: A provider sign-in is linked on email equality, so any identity provider that lets an attacker assert someone else's mailbox takes the local login over; or an email claim the provider never verified is trusted; or the authorization response is never bound to the request that began it, or arrives from a different issuer than the one the flow asked
Required Controls: Identity is issuer plus subject, never the address alone; an unverified email claim links nothing and grants nothing; bind the response to the request with a state and a nonce checked server-side against the session that started the flow; pin the issuer and the audience per provider and refuse a response from any other; linking a provider onto an existing local account is an identity mutation under its own row
Negative Tests: Test: a provider response carrying a known address but a different issuer or subject creates no link; an unverified email claim grants nothing; a response with a missing or replayed state is refused; a token minted for another audience is refused. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Abuse Case: The verifier accepts an unsigned algorithm, takes the verification key from the token's own header, skips the issuer audience or expiry check, or accepts an ID token where an access token was required
Required Controls: Pin the accepted algorithms and the key source server-side; never read a key or a key location out of the token; check issuer, audience, expiry and not-before on every request; keep ID tokens and access tokens distinct and refuse the wrong kind; call the library's verify entry point rather than decoding the payload and inspecting claims by hand
Negative Tests: Test: a token declaring no signature algorithm is refused; a token signed with a key named in its own header is refused; an expired token and a token for another audience are refused; an ID token presented as an access token is refused. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Abuse Case: An attacker makes the victim's browser log in to an account the attacker controls, so the victim's later activity accrues to it; the federated callback is the same shape when its state is not bound to the session
Required Controls: The login form and the federated callback carry a per-request anti-forgery token bound to the pre-login session; the session identifier rotates on login; the post-login landing performs no action on a cross-site request
Negative Tests: Test: a cross-site POST to the login endpoint without the bound token is refused; the session identifier differs before and after login. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own test suite

Threat: Signup abuse and disposable addresses as a policy choice
Source Refs: CWE-799, ASVS 5.0 V2 Validation and Business Logic
Abuse Case: Automated sign-up drains invites, trial credit, outbound mail reputation or a free tier; the reflex is a disposable-domain blocklist that also shuts out privacy-conscious people and quietly becomes a third-party call on the registration path
Required Controls: State the product's posture first - allow, warn, challenge or block - because the right answer differs between a consumer product and a paid B2B one; this is a policy row and names no list: any blocklist or reputation feed is a consumer dependency the consumer owns and ages; never a synchronous third-party call per registration request - decide asynchronously and degrade to allow when the dependency is unreachable; throttle and cost the sign-up path itself; verification before privilege carries most of the weight a blocklist is reached for
Negative Tests: Test: registration completes with the reputation dependency unreachable; the posture is written down with the flow and the implemented outcome matches it; a scripted burst of sign-ups from one source is throttled. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - this is a product policy, not a defect class; the deciding check is the consumer's own written posture and test suite

Abuse Case: Authenticated user swaps an id in the request and reads/writes another user's object
Required Controls: Object-level ownership check in policy (never only route middleware); deny-by-default
Negative Tests: Test: user A GET/PUT on B's resource id → 403/404, for EVERY verb

Abuse Case: Attacker posts role/is_admin fields the endpoint binds blindly
Required Controls: Explicit allowlist DTO/fillable; server-side role assignment only via admin flow
Negative Tests: Test: POST with role=admin → field ignored AND audit-logged

Abuse Case: Missing tenant_id scope on a query/report/export leaks another tenant's rows
Required Controls: Global scope at the ORM/repository layer; tenant from session never from request; scoped test fixtures
Negative Tests: Test: tenant A token + tenant B resource id across list/show/export/report → empty/403

Abuse Case: Queued job re-resolves tenant from payload an attacker influenced
Required Controls: Jobs carry tenant context sealed at dispatch; consumer re-asserts scope before write
Negative Tests: Test: forged job payload with foreign tenant_id → rejected

Abuse Case: Attacker uploads webshell/polyglot accepted by extension-only check
Required Controls: Content-sniff + allowlist MIME; store outside webroot with random names; never execute; AV scan if executable risk
Negative Tests: Test: .php/.svg-with-script renamed .jpg → rejected or neutralized; direct URL fetch of stored file cannot execute

Abuse Case: URL-fetch feature pointed at cloud metadata / internal services
Required Controls: Deny private/link-local ranges post-DNS-resolution; scheme allowlist; egress proxy; response-size cap
Negative Tests: Test: http://169.254.169.254/ and DNS-rebinding host → blocked

Abuse Case: Attacker posts forged or replayed events to the webhook consumer
Required Controls: HMAC signature verification with rotation; timestamp tolerance window; idempotency key store
Negative Tests: Test: bad signature → 401; stale timestamp → rejected; duplicate event id processed once

Abuse Case: Unauthenticated endpoint hammered for DoS or bulk data harvest
Required Controls: Rate limit + cache; no expensive queries pre-auth; pagination caps; no PII in public responses
Negative Tests: Test: response carries rate-limit headers; page size capped server-side

Abuse Case: Parallel requests redeem the same credit/refund twice
Required Controls: DB-level constraint or SELECT FOR UPDATE / idempotency key on money mutations; ledger over mutable balance
Negative Tests: Test: N parallel redeems of one voucher → exactly one success

Abuse Case: Client-supplied price or currency trusted at checkout
Required Controls: Recompute amounts server-side from catalog; signed cart or server-held cart only
Negative Tests: Test: tampered client amount → server total unchanged

Threat: Secret leakage via logs / errors / VCS
Abuse Case: Key appears in exception payload, debug log, or committed .env
Required Controls: Centralized secret manager; logger redaction list; pre-commit secret scan; scoped short-lived tokens
Negative Tests: Test: forced exception on auth path → no credential substring in log sink

Abuse Case: Serializer returns internal fields (cost, flags, foreign tenant refs) the UI ignores but attackers read
Required Controls: Explicit field allowlist per resource; separate admin vs public serializers; contract test on response shape
Negative Tests: Test: schema-diff response against documented contract → no undocumented fields

Threat: Unrestricted ingress to a management or database port
Abuse Case: Attacker reaches SSH/RDP or a database engine straight from the internet because a security-group or firewall rule allows 0.0.0.0/0
Required Controls: Deny-by-default ingress; management and database ports reachable only via bastion, VPN, or private link; CIDR scoped to known ranges; never 0.0.0.0/0 on 22/3389/3306/5432/6379/27017
Negative Tests: Test: a rule with cidr_blocks 0.0.0.0/0 on a management or database port is rejected. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - nothing here parses HCL or cloud config; the deciding check is the consumer's own IaC policy scanner

Abuse Case: Bucket or container created without a block-public-access setting so any object URL is world-readable
Required Controls: Block public access at account AND bucket level; explicit policy allowlist instead of a public ACL; serve objects via signed URLs or a CDN origin identity
Negative Tests: Test: storage created with no explicit public-access block is rejected; anonymous GET of a stored object returns 403. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own IaC policy scanner or a cloud posture tool

Threat: Missing encryption at rest or in transit
Abuse Case: Volume snapshot bucket or database instance created with no encryption block; endpoint accepts a plaintext connection
Required Controls: Encryption block mandatory on every storage and database resource; customer-managed key where the data class requires it; TLS-only bucket policy and listener; reject plaintext listeners
Negative Tests: Test: a storage or database resource with no encryption block is rejected; a plaintext connection to the endpoint is refused. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - the deciding check is the consumer's own IaC policy scanner

Abuse Case: A role policy grants Action * or Resource * so one compromised workload credential reaches every service and object in the account
Required Controls: Enumerate actions and resource ARNs; one role per workload; permission boundary or service control policy on privileged roles; no wildcard outside a named reviewed exception
Negative Tests: Test: a policy document containing Action "*" or Resource "*" is rejected or carries a named exception. Decided by: NO CHECK IN THIS REPOSITORY - nothing here parses IAM policy documents; the deciding check is the consumer's own IaC policy scanner

Threat: Credential in an IaC or vars file instead of a secret manager
Abuse Case: Password token or key written as a literal into a .tf .tfvars or .yaml file and committed
Required Controls: Secret-manager reference or runtime-injected env var; never a literal in IaC or vars files; treat the state file as sensitive and store it encrypted with restricted access
Negative Tests: Test: a literal credential in a tracked IaC or vars file fails the build. Decided by: check_secret_leak (src/scripts/check_secret_leak.ts) inside THIS repository - it has no extension allowlist so .tf and .yaml are in scope; for a CONSUMER the deciding check is the gitleaks workflow the package ships as a template that the consumer must copy
